issues.title: pipeline_snapshot: stop firing 9 GraphQL lists per repo root; use the ETag REST listing and bound fan-out
issues.body:
Part of #9243 · ADR-0021 amendment step 1 (PR #9250).

## Problem

`pipeline_snapshot::GhPipelineSource::fetch` (served by `loom-daemon serve`'s `GET /api/pipeline`) is probably the largest in-tree GraphQL amplifier (#9243):

- `PipelineMetrics::ALL` (what `serve.rs` constructs) fires **9** `gh issue list` / `gh pr list --limit 500` queries **per repo root**. All are GraphQL; none use the `--cached` REST/ETag path.
- `collect_pipeline_snapshots` fans out over **every** managed root, one `spawn_blocking` each, with **no concurrency bound**.
- It is fronted only by `PIPELINE_CACHE_TTL = 20s` (`serve.rs`).

At ~58 roots that is ~522 GraphQL requests per cache miss, so about a dozen misses exhaust a 6,550/hr pool. Any dashboard left open polling `/api/pipeline` does this continuously.

This is the largest violation of `forge_cmd.rs`'s own rule: use the `gh-cached` / `$GH_READ` helper wherever you would otherwise write a raw `gh issue list` in a hot path.

## Ask

- Serve the issue-side counts from the REST + ETag cached listing (`forge_listing` / `forge_cached_list`) instead of GraphQL `gh issue list`. Where a PR metric genuinely needs a shape the REST path can't serve, fold the 9 queries into as few calls per root as possible (e.g. one open-issues and one open-PRs listing, counted client-side by label).
- Bound the per-root fan-out, e.g. a small semaphore.
- Raise `PIPELINE_CACHE_TTL` to something proportionate to a dashboard (e.g. 60–120s), and document why.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `/api/pipeline` cache miss for N roots issues at most ~2 forge calls per root, and unchanged roots are served by `304`s. Covered by a test with a stub `gh`.
- [ ] Fan-out concurrency is bounded and the bound is tested.
- [ ] `/api/pipeline` response shape unchanged (dashboard keeps working).
- [ ] The PR body notes whether anything on the fleet hosts actually polls `/api/pipeline` (the cheap check #9243 asks for).


---

issues.title: pre-commit: scan staged content for credential shapes (no path-based defence covers an unpredicted path)
issues.body:
## Problem

`.githooks/pre-commit` (active via `core.hooksPath`) only runs Biome and
rustfmt. Nothing inspects **staged content** for credential-shaped strings.

Every credential defence Loom has today is **path-based**: `.gitignore`,
`land-resync-commit.sh`'s `LOOM_CREDENTIAL_PATTERNS`, `resync-installed.sh`'s
`:!` pathspec, and `CREDENTIAL_PATTERNS` in
`loom-daemon/src/init/post_init.rs`. They protect the paths we predicted. A
credential that reaches a path nobody enumerated is invisible to all of them
simultaneously, because they all consult the same literal list.

Two gaps make this the missing layer rather than a nice-to-have:

1. **A manual `git add -A` touches none of the script guards.** Those guards
   live inside `land-resync-commit.sh` / `resync-installed.sh`. A hand-rolled
   `git add -A && git commit` never invokes either, so their refusals cannot
   fire.
2. **CI-based scanning does not cover the case.** A commit pushed directly to
   `main` (see the companion ruleset-bypass issue) runs no PR checks at all.
   Adding gitleaks to CI would leave exactly this path uncovered.

A content scan is the only layer immune to both: it does not care what the
path is called, and it runs on the commit itself.

## Proposal

Extend `.githooks/pre-commit` with a staged-content scan that refuses the
commit when a staged blob matches a credential shape (`sk-ant-oat…`,
`sk-ant-api…`, `ghp_`/`github_pat_`, `tskey-auth-`, `AKIA`, `xox[baprs]-`,
`-----BEGIN … PRIVATE KEY`).

Design constraints:

- **Fixture noise is the hard part.** This repo legitimately contains fake
  secrets in at least: `defaults/scripts/tests/test-spawn-claude-credential-proxy.sh`,
  `loom-daemon/src/activity/session_analysis.rs`,
  `loom-daemon/src/activity/session_summary.rs`,
  `loom-daemon/src/credential_preflight.rs`,
  `loom-daemon/src/tokens_pool/check.rs`,
  `loom-daemon/src/worker_spawn/egress_proxy/exec_tests.rs`,
  `loom-daemon/tests/collector_fanout.rs`.
  All are obviously synthetic (`fake-real-token`, `SECRETKEYVALUE000000000`,
  `LOOMFIXTURE`, `…should-never-leak`). Needs an entropy floor, a marker
  allowlist, or both — a hook that cries wolf gets `--no-verify`'d into
  irrelevance, which is the failure mode to avoid.
- Reuse the shape list from one source of truth if practical, so it cannot
  drift the way the path lists did.
- Hook must stay fast; scan staged blobs only, never history.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Committing a file containing a realistic `sk-ant-oat01-…` value fails
      the pre-commit hook, **regardless of the file's path**.
- [ ] `git commit` on the current tree (all seven fixture files above staged)
      succeeds with no warning.
- [ ] Hook adds < 1s to a typical commit.
- [ ] Documented in `defaults/docs/guard-hooks.md`, including the explicit
      caveat that `--no-verify` bypasses it and that the hook requires
      `core.hooksPath=.githooks` to be set on the host.

## Non-goals

Replacing the path-based defences — this is an added layer, not a substitute.

issues.title: auto_update: bound the unsatisfiable-roll suppression with a cooldown retry, instead of waiting for a 900s-sampled in_flight == 0
issues.body:
## Context
<!-- loom:complexity=routine -->

Follow-up from the Judge's non-blocking item 2 on #9004 (which closed #8998).

#9004 stops the 21-hour arm → refuse → retain → abandon → re-arm livelock by declaring a roll's wait condition **unsatisfiable** and suppressing further re-arms. The suppression is sticky and clears on exactly one event: an auto-update tick that *samples* `in_flight == 0`.

That clearing condition is materially harder to hit than it reads:

- It is **sampled**, not continuous — once every `autonomous.autoUpdate.intervalSecs` (default `900`, `DEFAULT_AUTO_UPDATE_INTERVAL_SECS`).
- It is sampled **with dispatch running**. The drain's own quiescence watch is continuous *and* runs with dispatch paused, so in-flight there can only fall. After abandonment dispatch resumes, and a cap-12 dispatcher refills the in-flight set as soon as the long sweep ends.

On a busy host, a 900s sample can therefore miss every lull, and the host stops auto-updating for an **unbounded** time with no time-based retry. #9004 is still a strict improvement (the counterfactual host never updated *and* also lost dispatch, and the reason is now named loudly), which is why this was not blocking — but "unbounded paused dispatch" was traded for "unbounded staleness", not for a bounded state.

## The distinction that matters

A cooldown that re-arms once every N hours is **bounded**. The livelock was **unbounded**. That is the property worth having.

## Proposed direction

Add a bounded retry to `RollStallTracker` (`loom-daemon/src/auto_update/roll_stall.rs`) so a standing declaration expires on time as well as on an idle observation:

1. A new knob (`autonomous.autoUpdate.rollStallCooldownSecs` / `LOOM_AUTO_UPDATE_ROLL_STALL_COOLDOWN_SECS`, `env > config > default`, zero/invalid dropped like every sibling) — a plausible default is several hours, long enough that one retry per long sweep is the worst case.
2. When the declaration has stood for that long, clear it and let the next tick arm a roll normally. If the host still cannot drain, the detector re-declares after `rollStallDeadlines` more deadlines, so the cost is one bounded paused-dispatch budget per cooldown period rather than a continuous one.
3. Keep the `in_flight == 0` clear as the fast path.
4. Decide whether the retry should also relax the sampling problem (e.g. remember whether in-flight was *ever* seen at zero between ticks) or whether the cooldown alone is enough — the cooldown is the simpler property to reason about and probably sufficient.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A standing unsatisfiability declaration clears after a bounded, configurable period even if `in_flight == 0` is never sampled.
- [ ] The knob follows `env > config > default` with zero/invalid dropped on both sides, like `rollStallDeadlines`.
- [ ] A host that still cannot drain re-declares rather than cycling — i.e. the retry is bounded *per cooldown*, not a return to the #8998 livelock. Pin this with a test that runs several cooldown periods and asserts the number of paused-dispatch budgets consumed.
- [ ] `defaults/docs/daemon-reference.md` § "Scheduled drain-and-restart" replaces the current "no time-based retry … can stay un-updated indefinitely" caveat with the bounded behaviour.
- [ ] Unit-testable without a live daemon, clock-injected, in the existing `roll_stall.rs` style.

## Not in scope

#8998's directions 2 and 3 (age-excluding a long sweep from the drain condition; dropping the full-drain requirement for artifact rolls) — those are what would let a permanently-busy host actually roll, and each deserves its own design pass.

Refs: #9004, #8998, #6007, #8514

issues.title: ci-telemetry: poll several owners (orgs AND user accounts) so rjwalters/loom CI runs join story traces
issues.body:
## Problem

CI stitching into the D32 story trace (#9117) only happens for runs the CI poller sees. The poller captures a **single org**: `autonomous.ciTelemetry.org` (default `2amlogic`, `LOOM_CI_TELEMETRY_ORG`). It discovers repos with `GET /orgs/{org}/repos` (`ci_telemetry/poll.rs:~608`).

- **Loom's own CI is never captured.** `rjwalters/loom` is under a *user* account, so `/orgs/rjwalters/repos` does not apply. No story trace for a loom issue can contain a `loom.ci.run` span.
- **Measured 2026-09-27:** zero `loom.ci.run` spans in SigNoz in the last 3 days. The first derived story trace, `rjwalters/loom#9168` (trace `cf0ca10ca26dae948c2f6ac12ae45d19`, emitted by 2AMLogic/2am's storyline reconciler), has root, intake, queue_dwell, review_wait and merge spans, and no CI.

## Proposal

- Accept a list of **owners**. Add a new `autonomous.ciTelemetry.owners: ["2amlogic", "rjwalters"]`, and keep `org` as a deprecated single-owner alias. The env override `LOOM_CI_TELEMETRY_OWNERS` is comma-separated.
- For each owner, resolve whether it is an org or a user once, via `GET /users/{owner}` `type`, and cache the result. Discover repos with `/orgs/{o}/repos?type=all` or `/users/{o}/repos?type=owner` accordingly.
- Keep the existing per-repo ETag cache, backoff, `excludedRepos` / `logCaptureExcludedRepos` policy (entries become `owner/repo`, which they already are) and the single-captain gate.
- `ci-telemetry status` lists each owner with its kind and repo count.
- API budget: one extra `GET /users/{owner}` per owner per daemon lifetime, and one discovery walk per owner per cycle (ETag, so usually 304).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Config parsing: `owners` list, `org` alias, env override, precedence env > config > default, plus a test for each.
- [ ] Discovery: a user owner uses `/users/{u}/repos`, an org owner uses `/orgs/{o}/repos`. Both are covered by tests using the existing fake `GithubApi`.
- [ ] Existing `org`-only configs behave exactly as before (regression test).
- [ ] `defaults/docs/ci-observability.md` documents `owners`.

Part of #9037. Enabling the poller on a host (captain + `enabled=true`) remains an operator step.

issues.title: merge-pr.sh discards the daemon's fail-closed reason on exit 2, so the #8844 troubleshooting entry's symptom text never appears
issues.body:
Found while reviewing PR #8871 (#8844). The plan-gate fix itself is correct; this is
about the **residual fail-closed path**'s diagnosability, which that fix deliberately
preserves and now documents.

## Observed

`defaults/scripts/merge-pr.sh:1088` (`_check_required_check_freshness`) captures the
daemon's **stdout** into `$msg`, then unconditionally overwrites it whenever
`rc != 1`:

```bash
msg="$("${LOOM_DAEMON_BIN:-loom-daemon}" merge-pr stale-checks ...)" || rc=$?
[[ $rc -eq 0 && "$msg" == "LOOM-STALE-CHECKS-CLEAN" ]] && return 0
[[ $rc -eq 1 ]] || msg="Merge blocked: ... could not run — 'loom-daemon merge-pr stale-checks' exited $rc ..."
```

So on `rc=2` (the fail-closed "could not determine" verdict) the daemon's detailed
`unknown_message` — the one that quotes what the forge actually said — is thrown away.

Reproduced against the PR's own `merge-pr.sh`, with a stub daemon that prints the real
exit-2 message and exits 2:

```
$ # stub prints: "Merge blocked: ... ruleset lookup failed: gh: Upgrade to GitHub Pro
$ #               or make this repository public to enable this feature. (HTTP 403)"; exit 2
ERROR: Merge blocked: PR #8078's required-check freshness guard (#8248) could not run —
'loom-daemon merge-pr stale-checks' exited 2 without the LOOM-STALE-CHECKS-CLEAN signal.
... Build or install loom-daemon (cargo build --release -p loom-daemon, or re-run the
Loom installer), then re-run this merge.
```

The forge's reason is absent, and the remedy offered ("build or install loom-daemon")
is wrong for a lookup failure.

This is consistent with the retained suite: `defaults/scripts/tests/test-merge-pr-stale-required-checks.sh`
T3 asserts only `assert_contains "$LAST_OUT" "could not run"` — the daemon's stdout on
the exit-2 path is not asserted anywhere, because it does not survive.

## Consequence: two statements added by #8871 do not hold

1. `defaults/docs/troubleshooting.md` → "Every merge blocked by the freshness guard on a
   private free-plan repo (#8844)" shows a **Symptom** block quoting
   `... — ruleset lookup failed: gh: Upgrade to GitHub Pro ... (HTTP 403)`. `merge-pr.sh`
   never emits that string; an operator sees the generic "could not run" text above.
   The same section then says *"If you still see a block here, read the quoted forge
   error in the refusal"* — there is no quoted forge error to read. (The `gh api
   "repos/{owner}/{repo}/rules/branches/main"` reproduction command in that same
   paragraph does work, so the section is still actionable — just not by the route it
   describes.)
2. The new comment block at `defaults/scripts/merge-pr.sh:1055-1067` says dropping
   `2>/dev/null` means other failures "now print what the forge actually said". It does
   not: the daemon's reason goes to **stdout** (captured, then overwritten), and `gh`'s
   own stderr is captured inside the daemon by `Command::output()` in
   `loom-daemon/src/merge_pr/stale_checks/fetch.rs::gh_api`, so it never reaches the
   daemon's stderr either. The un-redirect does deliver the new `Warning:` notices on the
   CLEAN path (its primary purpose, correctly tested) and the shell's own
   "command not found" on a missing binary — but nothing on the `rc=2` path.

## Suspected fix shape (unverified — pick one)

- **Behavioural (preferred):** keep the daemon's stdout in the refusal on `rc >= 2`,
  e.g. append the captured `$msg` to the generic text rather than replacing it, and make
  the "build or install loom-daemon" remedy conditional on `rc=127`/empty output. Note
  `merge-pr.sh` is at its file-size-ratchet ceiling (`file-size-policy.md`), so this
  needs to be byte-frugal. Add a `test-merge-pr-stale-required-checks.sh` case pinning
  that the forge reason survives to the operator.
- **Documentation-only:** correct the troubleshooting Symptom block to the message
  merge-pr.sh actually prints, drop the "read the quoted forge error in the refusal"
  instruction (keep the `gh api` reproduction), and fix the `merge-pr.sh` comment's
  claim.

The first is worth more: the whole safety argument for the narrow `is_plan_gated`
predicate is "if GitHub rewords the message we fail closed again, which is the safe
direction" — and that path is exactly the one whose refusal currently names neither the
forge nor the real remedy.

Related: #8844, PR #8871, #8872 (the shell-twin plan gate), #8191 (merge-pr.sh → daemon port).

issues.title: Credential discovery convention for task agents: reference-by-name from the owner environment + explicit provisioning flow
issues.body:
**Credential discovery convention for task agents: reference-by-name from the owner environment, with an explicit provisioning flow for missing credentials**

## Problem

Agents working issue-driven tasks often need credentials for things *outside* Loom's own plumbing: cloud provider tokens, SSH identities, service API keys, per-host env files. Today Loom's config tiers (`env > .loom-project > .loom-local > default`, per `docs/design/config-resolution-tiers.md`) cover Loom's own needs — `forge.*`, `safehouse.*`, `observability.ingestKeyFile` — but there is no first-class convention for the **task credential surface**.

Consequences observed in practice (harness-ops, INFRA-08 / turian/harness-ops#189, 2026-09):

1. **Discovery burden falls entirely on repo docs.** In that repo, *every* live credential was already available in the owner environment (session-exported env vars; owner-only `0600` store under `~/.config/harness-ops/`). The agent self-served all of them — but only because the repo's runbooks document each reference *by name* (a "Where secrets and state live" section + a decision entry). That documentation must be authored per repo, per credential, and Loom neither encodes nor enforces the pattern. Omit it, and the same task class re-discovers (or re-asks about) credentials each session.
2. **The failure mode is asking the operator for values.** Without a documented lookup convention, an agent either stumbles interactively ("what's the SSH private key path?") or — worse — gets values pasted into the transcript/PR. Both break the "your only job: write issues, review PRs" model at exactly the moment an agent needs a key to progress.
3. **Provisioning is ad-hoc.** The good pattern that did work in that session: the owner authored a `0600` keys file containing *public-key material only* with `label:` lines, and the agent installed it idempotently by blob — the secret value (the *private* key) never touched the agent, and even the labels never landed on the host. Loom has no named shape for this "owner provisions, agent references by name" flow, so every repo reinvents it.

## Ask

A documented convention (optionally a committed manifest, like `.loom/credentials.md`, written by the repo owner, **names only — never values**) with a Loom-side policy that role prompts carry:

1. **Reference by name.** The manifest lists, per purpose: the env var name *or* owner-store file path *or* "provisioned file: <path>", plus usage rules: pull into the process env / read in-session, **never print, never commit, never quote in issue/PR text; report names only.**
2. **Lookup-before-ask rule.** Role prompts instruct the agent: when a task requires a credential, consult the repo's credential manifest first; only a *missing* credential may trigger an operator interaction, and that interaction requests the **name, shape, and provisioning path** — never the value.
3. **Standard provisioning flow.** The documented shape for new credentials is the demonstrated one above: owner writes a `0600` file (public material or env snippet) and/or an env export; agent verifies by name/checksum, installs idempotently, and reports only the outcome. This mirrors how Loom already treats host-local secrets (`forge.gitea.token` → `.loom-local`, "a raw token belongs host-local, never committed") but extends the principle to the task surface.

## Why named rather than value-carrying

- Agents run under the owner's uid: reading a `0600` file is legitimate; *printing or committing* the value is the hazard. A name-reference convention makes the diff between the two explicit and auditable.
- It keeps Loom's committed surface value-free (consistent with the existing "never committed" tiering) while making discovery *cheap*: one committed file lists the whole credential surface.

## Acceptance criteria (suggested)

- `docs/` carries the convention (e.g., `docs/credentials.md`), linked from the installed `AGENTS.md`/`CLAUDE.md` payload.
- Role prompts (or the base agent prompt) carry the lookup-before-ask + names-only rules.
- The `.loom` installer emits a names-only template (`.loom/credentials.md.example`) — with placeholders only, mirroring how this repo allows `*.env.example` in-tree.
- A short worked example (cloud token + SSH public-key provisioning) in the doc.

## Evidence pointers

- harness-ops conventions: `docs/decisions.md` D11 (no credentials in the repo working tree; names-only references) and `docs/runbooks/signoz-env.md` (§ "Where secrets and state live", § "a1 relay env — converged 2026-09-24") — the pattern working today as pure repo documentation.
- The provisioning flow described above shipped as `signoz-ssh-keys` in turian/harness-ops#189 (owner `0600` keys file, `label:` lines, idempotent by key blob, label never lands on the host).
- Loom's existing tiering: `docs/design/config-resolution-tiers.md` (host-local secret treatment for `forge.gitea.token`, `observability.ingestKeyFile`).

issues.title: merge-pr.sh: bare "${flags[@]}" under set -u breaks the loom:pr guard on stock macOS bash 3.2
issues.body:
## Environment

- macOS (darwin arm64), stock Apple `/bin/bash` **3.2.57** — the only bash on the machine before a Homebrew install
- `merge-pr.sh` as installed by Loom into a consumer repo (2AMLogic/loom-ui), current as of 2026-09-29
- `loom-daemon` 0.19.498 (83abe1f9) on PATH

## What happens

`./.loom/scripts/merge-pr.sh <N> --auto` fails closed on a fully mergeable PR:

```
./.loom/scripts/merge-pr.sh: line 853: flags[@]: unbound variable
Error: Merge blocked: PR #360's loom:pr review-signal guard (#7419) could not run —
'loom-daemon merge-pr loom-pr-guard' exited 1 without a recognized verdict.
```

The PR carries a valid `loom:pr` whose verdict SHA matches the head, and running the guard by hand exits 0 with `LOOM-PR-GUARD-CLEAN`. Re-running the identical script command under bash 5.3 (Homebrew) merges immediately. So the guard and daemon are fine — the guard *call* never happens on bash 3.2.

## Root cause

`_check_loom_pr_label` expands `"${flags[@]}"` unconditionally (line 853 of the installed copy, in `defaults/scripts/merge-pr.sh`):

```bash
msg="$(printf '%s\n' "$PR_LABELS" | "${LOOM_DAEMON_BIN:-loom-daemon}" merge-pr loom-pr-guard --pr "$PR_NUMBER" --head-sha "$PR_HEAD_SHA" "${flags[@]}" 2>/dev/null)" || rc=$?
```

Under `set -u`, bash < 4.4 treats an expansion of an **empty** array as an unbound-variable error and aborts the command substitution. `flags` is empty unless `--allow-unapproved` was passed — the normal merge path — so on stock macOS bash the guard invocation dies before `loom-daemon` ever runs, `rc` becomes non-zero, and the fail-closed branch refuses the merge.

The script already knows this hazard and defends everywhere else with the `${flags[@]+"${flags[@]}"}` idiom — e.g. the `head-sync-retry` call site and the `delete-branch` call site (line 2636). Line 853 is the one bare expansion left (I grepped: it is the only `"${flags[@]}"` in the file, and no other possibly-empty array is expanded bare).

## Suggested fix

Use the same defensive idiom the file already uses at its other daemon call sites:

```bash
... --head-sha "$PR_HEAD_SHA" ${flags[@]+"${flags[@]}}" 2>/dev/null)" || rc=$?
```

(quoted inner form, matching line 2636's style), or alternatively add `flags=()`-style initialization plus a documented bash ≥ 4 requirement — but since the file already carries 3.2-compat idioms elsewhere, the one-line idiom fix is the consistent choice.

## Notes

- Repro: stock macOS bash + any `loom:pr` PR + `--auto` (the flags array is empty without `--allow-unapproved`), merge blocked regardless of review state.
- The error text ("Build or install loom-daemon…") sent me rebuilding the daemon and re-checking auth — the actual problem was the caller's shell. A guard-fault message that can't distinguish "binary missing" (rc 127) from "array expansion aborted before exec" (bash 3.2) cost a debug cycle; worth a look if the fail-closed branch ever gets instrumented.

issues.title: install/upgrade never verifies the repo's merge configuration — a ruleset can make merge-pr.sh structurally unable to merge, silently
issues.body:
## What happened here, in this repo

For most of 2026-09-27→28 **nothing could merge**, and every diagnostic looked healthy.

The repo settings were correct: `allow_merge_commit=true`, `allow_squash_merge=false`, `allow_rebase_merge=false` — the merge-commit default ADR-0022 sets. But the `main` ruleset (id `8809610`, `enforcement: active`) carried:

- `pull_request.allowed_merge_methods = ["squash"]` — the one method the repo forbids, and
- a `required_linear_history` rule, which rejects a merge commit even when the method *is* permitted.

The intersection of "methods the repo allows" and "methods the ruleset allows" was **empty**. Every `merge-pr.sh` call returned `405 Merge commits are not allowed`. It was not total, which is why it took a while to spot: the ruleset's two bypass actors kept merging normally while everyone else failed, so the queue built to roughly twenty approved PRs — including an ADR amendment — before anyone connected the failures.

Fixed by setting the ruleset to `["merge"]` and dropping `required_linear_history`.

## Why this is an install/upgrade concern, not just an ops mistake

`merge-pr.sh` is Loom's merge path. Its ability to function depends on **forge-side configuration that lives outside the repo tree**, that nothing in Loom reads, and that Loom's own install and resync never look at. A consumer can install Loom into a repo whose merge configuration makes `merge-pr.sh` structurally incapable of merging, and Loom will report a clean install and only fail much later — at the end of a Builder→Judge→merge cycle, which is the most expensive possible place to discover it.

The failure is also silent in the direction that matters. Nothing warns; the first symptom is a 405 several phases downstream, attributed to the PR rather than the repo.

## The precedent already exists

Loom already verifies forge-side state at install/upgrade — this is the same class, not a new one:

- `check-labels-drift.sh` reads the repo's **live label set** from the forge and reports drift from the shipped set.
- `check-guards-installed.sh` verifies the guard hooks are actually wired.
- `check-git-identity.sh`, `check-config-no-host-paths.sh`, and the rest of the `check-*.sh` family cover the local half.

But `install.sh` performs **no forge-side repo-config verification at all** (grepped for `allow_merge_commit`, `allow_squash`, `merge_method`, `ruleset`, `gh api repos/` — nothing). Labels are checked because a missing label breaks the pipeline. The merge configuration breaks the pipeline harder, and is unchecked.

## Proposed: `check-merge-config.sh`, run at install and at resync

Compute the **effective merge-method set** for the default branch:

```
effective = {methods the repo allows}
            ∩ {allowed_merge_methods of every ACTIVE branch ruleset targeting the default branch}
```

Report when:

1. **`effective` is empty** — no permitted method exists. Every merge will 405. (This incident.)
2. **`required_linear_history` is active AND `merge` is the only member of `effective`** — the one permitted method is structurally rejected by a sibling rule. Same outcome, different cause.
3. **`effective` excludes the method this install is configured to use** — the narrower, more common version of (1).

Three things that decide whether this is useful or gets muted:

- **Rulesets AND together.** A branch can carry several active rulesets; the permitted set is the intersection of all of them, not the union. Any implementation that reads only the first ruleset will be wrong on a repo that has two.
- **`required_linear_history` with squash is CORRECT, not a finding.** Squash produces linear history, and that pairing is common and deliberate. A blanket "linear history is bad" rule false-positives on ordinary repos and gets the whole check disabled. Only flag it against a `merge`-only effective set.
- **A repo with no ruleset must behave exactly as today.** No new output, no new failure mode — most repos have none.

**Advisory, not fatal, at install time.** This mirrors the existing pre-wave advisory contract (`check-host-sleep.sh`, `check-main-freshness.sh`): report loudly, always exit 0, never block an install over forge configuration the installer may not have permission to read or change. Reading rulesets can 403 on a credential with push but not admin — that is "unknown", not "broken", and must not fail the install or be reported as a finding.

**Never auto-repair.** A ruleset is a deliberate protection artifact. Reporting it is right; silently rewriting one from an installer is not — the remedy needs a named human, which is exactly what did happen here.

## Suggested acceptance criteria

- [ ] `defaults/scripts/check-merge-config.sh` computes the effective merge-method set as defined above.
- [ ] It reports cases 1–3; it stays silent on a repo with no ruleset, and on `required_linear_history` paired with a squash-capable effective set.
- [ ] Multiple active rulesets on one branch intersect correctly.
- [ ] A 403 reading rulesets reports "could not determine", never a finding, and never fails.
- [ ] Always exits 0. It never blocks an install, an upgrade, or a resync.
- [ ] `install.sh` and `resync-installed.sh` both invoke it, alongside the existing drift checks.
- [ ] It never writes a ruleset or a repo setting.
- [ ] Consider surfacing it as a `/loom:sweep` pre-wave advisory too — a sweep that will dispatch Builders into a repo that cannot merge should say so before spending the cycles, not after.

<!-- Filed by an attended operator session, 2026-09-28, after diagnosing and fixing the ruleset deadlock described above. -->

Scope, integration points, and acceptance criteria corrected/tightened in the

below — read that comment before implementing; it supersedes the
"install.sh...invoke it" line above and narrows this issue to the

issues.body:
## Observed

On `main`, CI run 36249734448 (commit `6496cd19b`, a "resync installed Loom surfaces" commit touching no Rust) failed one test in the job **Rust OTLP Feature Tests (1/3)**, job 108425397571:

```

  test_socket_pidfile_and_heartbeat_are_ready_during_slow_startup_reconciliation
panicked at loom-daemon/tests/integration_startup_reconciliation_gate.rs:182:5
```

The next `main` run (36249854634) passed.

## Why it is probably load-sensitive, not a regression

The assertion at `:182` is a latency bound: the socket must bind in under `STUB_DELAY / 2`. The halving is meant to "tolerate ordinary scheduling jitter on a loaded CI host". Two changes landed just before this run and raise the load on a runner:

- **#9069 partitioned nextest into 3 legs.** Each leg still runs 4 test threads on 4 vCPUs. The `daemon-integration` group still serialises integration tests within a leg, but which unit tests share the runner with them changed.
- **#9069's `wait -n` fix** made shell suites genuinely 4-wide. That's a different job, so it doesn't affect this one directly.

A wall-clock bound compared against a fraction of a stub delay will flake whenever the runner is busy enough. This is the #7789 class.

## Suggested fix (pick one)

1. **Assert ordering, not wall time.** Check that the bind, pidfile and first heartbeat happen *before* the stubbed pass signals completion, for example by making the stub wait on a barrier the test releases only after its checks. That tests the #7974 claim ("ready WHILE the pass is sleeping") without a timing race.
2. Or lengthen `STUB_DELAY` and keep the fraction. Cheaper, but it only moves the flake threshold.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The test no longer depends on a wall-clock fraction of `STUB_DELAY`, or the flake is shown to be gone over 20 consecutive CI runs.
- [ ] The #7974 regression is still caught: if the socket bind reverted to waiting for the startup pass, the test fails deterministically.

Related: #7789 (flake tracking), #9065 / #9069 (CI partitioning), #9089 (per-test spans, which would show this test's duration trend).

---

## Curator Enhancement

Full `## Affected Files`, `## Test Plan`, and related-work disposal (#9065/#9089) added in the Curator comment on this issue, 2026-09-28.

issues.title: check-runs reads outside forge_get_check_runs can still truncate (Gitea branch, daemon stale-checks guard)
issues.body:
Found while implementing #8895 (PR #8986), which fixed the GitHub branch of `forge_get_check_runs` (`per_page=100` + `--paginate`, plus a fail-closed rc when the row count is short of `total_count`). Two other reads of the same endpoint class were deliberately left out of that PR's scope.

## 1. `forge_get_check_runs`, Gitea branch

`defaults/scripts/lib/forge-helpers.sh` — the Gitea branch makes ONE unpaginated request:

```
gitea_api GET "repos/$FORGE_OWNER/$FORGE_REPO/commits/$commit/statuses"
```

Gitea caps a page at `MAX_RESPONSE_ITEMS` (50 by default, `DEFAULT_PAGING_NUM` 30), so the same 30-row truncation class applies. Worse, this branch derives `total_count` from the rows it received (`total_count: (. | length)`), so the fail-closed short-read check the GitHub branch now has is structurally unable to fire here — a truncated read looks self-consistent.

The library already has `_forge_gitea_paginate` (used by `forge_get_pr_reviews`), which fails closed on a pagination failure and refuses to report a truncated list. Restructuring this branch to use it (per-row jq filter + `jq -s` to rebuild the `{total_count, check_runs}` rollup) is the fix. Note `defaults/scripts/lib/forge-helpers.sh` is at its file-size baseline (1011 code lines), so the change must be line-neutral or shrinking.

A `KNOWN GAP (Gitea)` comment on the helper's doc block points here.

## 2. `fetch_check_runs` in the daemon's stale-checks guard

`loom-daemon/src/merge_pr/stale_checks/fetch.rs` (~line 226) passes `per_page=100` but does **not** paginate, and its `--jq` drops `total_count` entirely, so there is nothing to compare a row count against:

```rust
&format!("repos/{nwo}/commits/{head_sha}/check-runs"),
"--method", "GET", "-f", "per_page=100", "--jq",
"[.check_runs[]? | {name: .name, status: .status, conclusion: .conclusion, started_at: .started_at, app: .app.slug, details_url: .details_url}]",
```

Less acute than #8895 (100 is above this repo's 39, and this feeds the stale-checks guard rather than the settle decision), but it is the same silent-subset shape: a repo that grows past 100 check-runs gets a guard evaluated on a subset with no signal that anything was missing. Fix shape: paginate, and keep `total_count` so a short read can fail closed the way the shell helper now does.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The Gitea branch of `forge_get_check_runs` retrieves every commit status for a commit (not one page), and a pagination failure returns nonzero rather than a short list.
- [ ] The daemon's `fetch_check_runs` paginates and fails closed (error, not a partial `Vec<CheckRun>`) when the retrieved count is short of the endpoint's `total_count`.
- [ ] Regression coverage for each: a multi-page fixture, and a short-read fixture asserting the fail-closed path.
- [ ] `defaults/scripts/lib/forge-helpers.sh` does not grow past its file-size baseline.

Either half is independently shippable; splitting into two PRs is fine.

---

## Curator Enhancement

<!-- loom:complexity=routine -->

Verified both gaps against `origin/main` @ `7e0a29b0d` (2026-09-27) — both match this issue's description exactly, no drift since filing. See curator comment below for the verification detail (file-size baseline, enumeration of other call sites, duplicate check).

### Affected Files

- `defaults/scripts/lib/forge-helpers.sh` - Restructure the Gitea branch of `forge_get_check_runs` (~line 561-590) to page through `commits/{sha}/statuses` via the existing `_forge_gitea_paginate` helper (already used by `forge_get_pr_reviews`) instead of one unpaginated call, and derive a real `total_count`/short-read check the way the GitHub branch already does (line 606-638) — line-neutral or shrinking overall, since the file is at its 1011-line baseline.
- `loom-daemon/src/merge_pr/stale_checks/fetch.rs` - Add pagination (mirroring the shell helper's `--paginate` fix from #8895) to `fetch_check_runs` (~line 269), and keep `total_count` through the `--jq` projection so a short read can fail closed instead of silently returning a `Vec<CheckRun>` subset.

### Test Plan

- [ ] Automated tests: add a multi-page Gitea `statuses` fixture (more rows than one page) asserting `forge_get_check_runs` returns the full merged set, not a truncated first page.
- [ ] Automated tests: add a short-read fixture for the Gitea branch (fewer rows returned than the forge's own count implies) asserting the function fails closed rather than returning a self-consistent-looking partial result.
- [ ] Automated tests: add equivalent multi-page and short-read fixtures for `fetch_check_runs` in `fetch.rs`, asserting pagination and a fail-closed error (not a partial `Vec<CheckRun>`) on a short read.
- [ ] Manual verification: run `defaults/scripts/lib/forge-helpers.sh`'s existing test suite (if any) plus `cargo test` in `loom-daemon` for the `merge_pr::stale_checks` module after the change.
- [ ] Verify `defaults/scripts/lib/forge-helpers.sh` line count has not grown past its `scripts/file-size-baseline.txt` entry (1011 lines).

issues.title: Champion critical-file hold deadlocks with merge-pr.sh's #8112 guard: the documented human merge path is refused and the hold re-arms after release
issues.body:
## Problem

Champion's critical-file hold and `merge-pr.sh`'s #8112 verdict-contradiction guard deadlock. The documented human release path doesn't work.

- Champion puts `loom:operator` on any approved PR that touches a critical-file pattern (e.g. `.github/workflows/`), **keeps `loom:pr`**, and says: *"this hold stays in force until … a human merges it directly with `./.loom/scripts/merge-pr.sh <N>`"*.
- `merge-pr.sh` refuses any PR carrying both `loom:pr` and `loom:operator` (#8112), with **no override flag** by design.
- If the human removes `loom:operator` first, Champion **re-adds it on its next tick**, even though the operator's release comment is already on the PR.

So a human-approved merge only works by racing Champion: remove the label and merge in the same shell command, and hope the required checks are still fresher than the base tip (#8248).

## Evidence: merge train #8996, 2026-09-26

The operator explicitly approved merging (the train touched `release.yml` and `ci.yml`). Label events for `loom:operator`:

```
04:46:30Z labeled   by loom-fleet-dispatch[bot]   (critical-file hold)
04:48:16Z unlabeled by operator session           (release comment posted)
04:49:58Z labeled   by loom-fleet-dispatch[bot]   (re-added, 1m42s later)
04:58:04Z unlabeled by operator session
```

The first attempt to merge after releasing the hold hit `merge-pr.sh`'s both-labels block again. It finally merged at 05:08Z, by removing the label and running `merge-pr.sh` in the same command right after a CI re-run.

## Proposal (pick one)

1. **Durable operator release marker.** Champion recognises a release comment/marker (e.g. `<!-- operator:critical-file-release head=<sha> -->`) bound to the current head SHA and doesn't re-hold that head. `merge-pr.sh` treats the same marker as resolving the contradiction for that SHA only.
2. **Champion removes `loom:pr` when it places a critical-file hold**, so the human path is `merge-pr.sh --allow-unapproved`, which already exists for exactly "a human asserts approval". This changes the hold comment's "keeping `loom:pr`" semantics.
3. **A distinct label** (e.g. `loom:critical-file-hold`) that `merge-pr.sh` treats as "requires a human-run merge" rather than as a contradictory verdict.

Whichever is chosen, the hold comment's "Next steps" must describe a path that actually works.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An operator can release a critical-file hold and merge with one documented, non-racy procedure.
- [ ] Champion doesn't re-hold a head the operator has released. A new push re-arms the hold.
- [ ] The #8112 guard still blocks a genuine Judge rejection racing an approval.
- [ ] Test covering release → Champion tick → merge.

Related: #8112, #8248, #6877 (merge-risk hold digest), #8996.

issues.title: Open-PR dispatch guard counts bare mentions: the daemon's timeline leg lacks the sweep's #6216 phrase filter, permanently starving #8322
issues.body:
## Problem

The daemon's #4123 open-PR dispatch guard and `/loom:sweep`'s existing-PR probe implement **the same question** — "does issue #N already have an open linked PR?" — and answer it differently. The daemon's version has no phrase filter, so **any** PR that merely mentions `#N` anywhere in its body or comments permanently refuses dispatch of `#N`.

When the mentioning PR is itself parked and never closes, the issue is starved forever.

## Root cause

`OPEN_LINKED_PR_TIMELINE_JQ` (`loom-daemon/src/worktree_ops/gh.rs:272`, shared with `sweep_registry::guards::probe_open_linked_pr_rest` per #8116):

```jq
[.[] | select(.event == "cross-referenced"
              and .source.issue.pull_request != null
              and .source.issue.state == "open"
              and .source.issue.repository.full_name == "{full_name}")
 | .source.issue.number] | unique | .[0] // empty
```

Its own doc comment states the behaviour plainly:

> GitHub emits a `cross-referenced` event for **any** PR body reference to the issue, so this is a strict superset of the closes-graph

The superset is intentional and correct in motivation — #7757/#7859/#8116 added the timeline leg so a `Part of #N` phase PR would be seen, which `closedByPullRequestsReferences` structurally cannot see. But the sweep skill solved the same problem **with a phrase filter** and the daemon did not.

`sweep-wave-lifecycle.md` → "Existing-PR probe", the `#6216` phrase filter:

```bash
gh pr view <pr_number> --json body --jq '.body // ""' \
  | grep -iqE "(Part of|Contributes to)[*_:[:space:]]*#N"
```

> Discard any candidate whose body does not match — it was a bare mention, not a partial-increment linkage, and **must not** count as an open linked PR.

So the two probes diverge exactly on a bare mention. The skill discards it; the daemon treats it as a linked PR and refuses dispatch.

## Confirmed live instance: #8322 starved for 6.5 days

**#8322** has been `loom:issue` + `loom:curated` since 2026-09-19T07:05Z, carried `loom:urgent` for most of that, and **never once reached `loom:building`** — no claim comment, no decline, no dispatch record of any kind in 6.5 days.

The cause: **PR #8314 mentions `#8322`** — Doctor's stand-down comment on #8314 reads "filed #8322 to track it, standing down without pushing." That comment creates a `cross-referenced` event on #8322's timeline whose source is open PR #8314. Running the daemon's exact jq against #8322 returns:

```
[8314]      # before this issue's own PR existed
[8314, 8939]  # now
```

#8314's actual closes-graph is `closingIssuesReferences = [8256]` — it does **not** close #8322. And #8314 is `loom:blocked` + `loom:changes-requested`, parked since 2026-09-19, so it will not close on its own. The refusal was therefore permanent.

Verified directly — `loom-daemon forge check-open-pr 8322` refuses the claim and names the mentioning PR. The refusal message is accurate about its own logic; the logic is what is wrong.

This was found because an in-session `/loom:sweep` **did** dispatch #8322 — its phrase filter correctly discarded #8314 as a bare mention — and the Builder then hit the daemon guard's contradictory answer from inside the same repo. The two probes disagreeing about the same issue at the same moment is the cleanest possible demonstration.

The cost here was concrete: #8322 gates PR #8314, which gates **#8256**, an urgent security issue (per-role tool-restriction allowlist enforced at the harness). Three artifacts, all urgent, stalled on a bare mention.

## Why this is a "designed twice" defect

`defaults/docs/` and the skill treat the phrase filter as part of the probe's definition (#6216 exists precisely because bare mentions were producing wrong answers). The daemon reimplements the probe without it. Per the repo's own reuse discipline, these should be one definition with one behaviour, not two that drift.

Note the daemon module already knows it is duplicating: `forge_check_open_pr.rs:22` says the closes-graph leg and the `Part of #N` timeline leg "are NOT reimplemented here; a divergence…". The phrase filter is the part that did not make the trip.

## Proposal

1. **Apply the `#6216` phrase filter to the daemon's timeline leg.** A timeline hit becomes a linked PR only when the source PR's body carries `Part of #N` / `Contributes to #N` (tolerant of markdown emphasis/colon, matching the skill's regex and `parse_dependencies`' convention). A bare mention is discarded.
2. **Keep the closes-graph leg unfiltered** — a `Closes #N` PR is a linked PR regardless of phrasing. Only the timeline leg needs the filter.
3. **Pin the divergence with a test** asserting a bare-mention PR does not refuse dispatch while a `Part of #N` PR does.
4. Consider whether the skill and the daemon can share one definition rather than two implementations.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] An open PR that mentions `#N` without a closing keyword or a `Part of`/`Contributes to` phrase does **not** cause the daemon to refuse dispatch of `#N`.
- [ ] An open PR with `Part of #N` / `Contributes to #N` still **does** (no regression on #7757/#7859/#8116).
- [ ] An open PR with `Closes #N` still does, via the closes-graph leg, unchanged.
- [ ] Regression test covers all three shapes.
- [ ] `loom-daemon forge check-open-pr <N>` and `/loom:sweep`'s existing-PR probe return the same verdict for the same issue — ideally enforced by a shared definition rather than parallel code.

## Notes

Filed from an in-session `/loom:sweep` run on #8322 (RUN_ID `sweep-20260925T164606Z-1948-00a73bd9`). The Builder that surfaced it flagged it as "a false positive… may be worth a separate issue against the guard's linkage heuristic" — this is that issue, with the mechanism confirmed in source.

Related: #8925 (blocked artifacts have no exit path) — #8314 being parked indefinitely is what made this refusal permanent rather than transient. The two defects compound: #8925 keeps the mentioning PR open forever, and this issue turns that into a dispatch refusal on a different issue.

issues.title: docs: state what Loom optimizes for — and that it is the wrong tool under time pressure (hackathon fit note)
issues.body:
## Problem

Loom's documentation explains *how* the system works in great detail, but nowhere
states *what it optimizes for* — or, just as importantly, when it is the wrong
tool. A new user reading the README sees "AI agents claim issues, implement
features, review PRs, and merge code" and reasonably infers that Loom's job is to
produce code fast. It isn't. Loom's job is to produce code that is correct when
nobody is watching it get produced.

That gap has a real cost. We attempted to use Loom during a hackathon on
2026-09-27, and the major learning was that the tool is not tuned for a
time-pressure situation. Every gate did exactly what it was designed to do, and
every gate was latency we could not afford. Nothing malfunctioned; the tool was
simply being used against its grain, and nothing in the docs warned us.

## The framing

The useful mental model: **Loom's gates are priced in human-attention units.**

Curator enrichment, Judge review, Doctor cycles, Champion merge-risk holds,
`buildGate`, and the "CI is dumb and reliable, on purpose" stance each buy a
specific guarantee — and each guarantee only pays for itself when no human is
watching the work happen. That is the actual design target: code produced 24/7
with very little human intervention, where a bad merge at 3am costs hours of
unattended compute chasing a broken `main`, and a Judge pass that catches it
costs ten minutes.

At a hackathon the economics invert completely. A human is watching
continuously and can catch breakage in seconds. The gates buy insurance against
a risk that is already covered, so they become pure latency with nothing bought
in return. "Loom felt slow at the hackathon" is therefore not a defect report —
it is a correct reading of a deliberate trade, applied in the one regime where
the trade is a bad deal.

Writing this down converts a surprise into a decision rule, and it does so
without apologizing for the design or promising to change it.

## Proposed change

Follow the repo's canonical-place-plus-pointers convention — one piece of
reasoning, two short signposts, no duplicated prose to drift.

**1. New canonical essay: `docs/philosophy/latency-vs-reliability.md`**

Sits alongside the existing essays (`agent-archetypes.md`, `ai-code-smell.md`,
`philosophy-of-vibe-coding.md`, `working-with-ai.md`) and should match their
register — an essay, not a reference table. It should cover:

- What Loom actually optimizes for: unattended correctness over long horizons,
  not time-to-first-working-thing.
- The attention-units framing above, as the load-bearing idea.
- What each gate buys, concretely — not a restatement of the pipeline, but a
  one-line "this exists because X goes wrong overnight" for Curator, Judge,
  Doctor, Champion merge-risk holds, and `buildGate`. Link to
  [`build-gate.md`](../../defaults/docs/build-gate.md) and
  [`ci-principles.md`](../../defaults/docs/ci-principles.md) rather than
  restating them.
- The regime where the trade is bad: short deadlines, disposable artifacts, a
  human watching continuously.
- An explicit alternative recipe for that regime, stated without hedging: work
  in live agent sessions rather than dispatching sweeps; write fewer tests;
  merge rapidly and skip the review round-trip; fix problems by over-patching
  rather than diagnosing root cause. The artifact's lifetime is measured in
  hours, so the debt never comes due — that is what makes the recipe correct
  there and wrong everywhere else.
- The 2026-09-27 hackathon as the concrete grounding case.

**2. README pointer** — a short block near the top (not a new bottom section;
the decision happens before install). Roughly: what Loom optimizes for in two
sentences, the "if you need to ship in hours, Loom is the wrong tool and here's
what to do instead" sentence, and a link to the essay. Keep it to a handful of
lines — the README is already 423 lines and the reasoning belongs in the essay.

**3. `docs/guides/getting-started.md` pointer** — a short subsection under
§"Before You Install", adjacent to the existing "What Loom Does". This is the
exact moment a reader is deciding whether to install, which makes it the highest-
value placement in the repo for a fit warning.

## Non-goals

- **This issue does not add a "yolo mode."** Fast-path / low-gate operation may
  be worth building someday, but it is explicitly not the current priority, and
  this issue is about documenting the design intent we already have — not
  changing it. A Builder picking this up should not implement, prototype, or
  design a gate-bypass flag. If the essay makes the case that such a mode should
  exist, that belongs in a separate proposal.
- No changes to gate behavior, defaults, config, or role prompts. This is
  docs-only.
- Not a rewrite of the existing philosophy essays.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `docs/philosophy/latency-vs-reliability.md` exists and covers: what Loom
      optimizes for, the attention-units framing, what each gate buys, the
      regime where the trade is bad, the explicit hackathon alternative recipe,
      and the 2026-09-27 hackathon as grounding.
- [ ] README contains a brief "what Loom optimizes for / when it's the wrong
      tool" block linking to the essay.
- [ ] `docs/guides/getting-started.md` §"Before You Install" contains a brief
      fit note linking to the essay.
- [ ] `docs/README.md`'s `philosophy/` row is updated to mention the new essay
      (that row currently enumerates the essays by topic).
- [ ] The essay's reasoning appears in exactly one place; the two pointers
      summarize and link rather than restate.
- [ ] No non-`.md` files are modified.
- [ ] Internal links resolve (`/repo:links` or equivalent passes).

## Notes for the Curator

The judgment call worth pinning down during curation is **tone**. This essay
should read as a confident statement of design intent, not as an apology for
slowness or a promise of a future fast mode. The hackathon story is evidence
that the design has a regime boundary — it is not a bug report, and it should
not be written as one.

## Affected Files

- `docs/philosophy/latency-vs-reliability.md` - new essay (create).
- `README.md` - add the short "what Loom optimizes for / when it's the wrong tool" pointer block near the top.
- `docs/guides/getting-started.md` - add a brief fit-note subsection under §"Before You Install".
- `docs/README.md` - update the `philosophy/` row to list the new essay.

## Test Plan

- [ ] Manual verification: read the new essay end-to-end and confirm it covers all six required elements from the Acceptance Criteria checklist above.
- [ ] Manual verification: confirm the README and getting-started pointers are brief (a handful of lines each), link to the essay, and do not duplicate its reasoning.
- [ ] Automated tests: N/A (docs-only change; no code tests apply).
- [ ] Link check: run `/repo:links` (or equivalent) to confirm all new/updated internal links resolve.
- [ ] Verify no non-`.md` files are touched (`git diff --name-only` against the PR).

issues.title: Champion: automatically order overlapping PRs and defer redundant base repairs (9063 first release)
issues.body:
## Parent and operator decision
Part of #9063. The operator selected automatic ordering of overlapping PRs plus recommendations for combinations as the first release. A reporting-only result does not complete this issue. Automatic combined PRs are later work.

## Problem and scope
When several PRs touch the same area, repairing each against every intermediate main tip can send the same work through Doctor and Judge repeatedly. Establish and honor a stable, per-repository landing order before doing redundant repairs.

Evaluate repositories with **more than two open PRs**, including those awaiting review. Count all open PRs for the trigger; drafts and existing holds remain ineligible for automatic landing. Explicit dependencies and operator priorities constrain the order; otherwise prefer a stable, oldest-first order within related/overlapping groups. Unrelated PRs continue independently. Shared filenames are evidence of possible overlap, not proof that two changes are semantically compatible.

Use the sequencing gate from #9378 rather than inventing another hold label or treating `loom:blocked` as a merge gate. Persist owner/repo, PR numbers, observed head/base SHAs, predecessor conditions and reasons in authenticated, machine-readable state, so independent Champion/Doctor invocations honor the same order. Add a concise, idempotent explanation and combination recommendation on affected PRs.

Defer only speculative/base-conflict-only repair behind an eligible predecessor. Genuine review feedback can still be fixed, existing active claims are respected, and Judge/CI/hold/freshness checks remain mandatory. Closed, held, stalled or changed predecessors require re-evaluation: soft scheduling preferences must not starve otherwise eligible work; true semantic dependencies must not expire into permission to merge. Recompute on relevant changes and prevent competing workers from applying incompatible plans.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] With three overlapping PRs, the order is persisted and enforced across separate role invocations; a follower is not merged early or repeatedly sent for base-only repair while its predecessor is making progress.
- [ ] An unrelated fourth PR can proceed, and repositories below the trigger retain normal behavior. The last needed repair still runs after predecessors land.
- [ ] Dependency/priority constraints, cycles, unavailable forge data, changed heads, active claims, held/stalled predecessors and abandoned plan ownership have explicit tested behavior.
- [ ] No substantive rejection is suppressed and no verdict or CI result is fabricated/carried forward by this feature. #9416 owns proven-equivalence approval carryover.
- [ ] Identical plans do not produce repeated comments. Expose plan identity, reason and defer/release events for later churn measurement.
- [ ] Demonstrate changed scheduling with an integration fixture covering multiple role passes, rather than only testing a recommendation string. Record a read-only replay against a real PR inventory before rollout.

## Dependencies
- Depends on #9378 for the durable merge sequencing gate; extend that primitive rather than duplicate it.
- #9062 is related rejection-attribution work, not a prerequisite for ordering.

## Implementation starting points
Verified paths on origin/main at 82891089530c721c6365033b2dde592302096c94 on 2026-09-30: `defaults/.claude/commands/loom/champion-pr-merge.md`, `defaults/.claude/commands/loom/doctor.md`, `loom-daemon/src/claim_reconciliation/review_conflict.rs`, and `loom-daemon/src/merge_pr/`. The conflict reconciler currently routes base conflicts to Doctor (module contract inspected); trace actual scheduling call sites before changing them. New executable policy belongs in Rust, with role prompts consuming it. Honor prompt-generation and pressure-test requirements. Do not edit installed copies as the source of truth.

The similarly named `work_finder::dispatch_plan_merge::merge_plans` merges observations from hosts, not pull requests; #9524 is not an implementation of this feature.

## Test plan
Deterministic order fixtures; multi-worker/changed-head scenarios; genuine-feedback versus base-only repair; held, closed and stalled predecessors; independent PR progress; repeat-pass idempotency; existing merge-guard regressions.

issues.title: Guide urgency_rank() rank-2 'outage' regex false-positives on component names (recurring, #8649)
issues.body:
## Problem

`guide.md`'s `urgency_rank()` ladder assigns rank 2 ("the delivery pipeline
itself is down") via a bare title-substring regex:

```
if printf '%s\n' "$title" | grep -Eqi 'broken main|main is red|CI is red|pipeline (is )?(stalled|halted|wedged)|outage'; then
  echo 2; return
fi
```

`outage` (and to a lesser extent `stalled`/`halted`) is a plausible substring
of a component *name*, not just a live-incident claim. Observed twice on the
same issue: #8649, "watchdog: peer-coord/**outage** sentinel writes silently
swallow I/O errors, causing duplicate escalation issues under disk pressure"
(`tier:maintenance`) — a real but routine reliability bug in escalation-dedup
bookkeeping, not an assertion that the pipeline is currently down.

- 2026-09-23 ~09:13 UTC: one fleet-host tick read the regex literally and
  promoted #8649 to `loom:urgent` on the strength of the false rank-2 match.
- 2026-09-23 ~09:26 UTC: a manual triage session recognized the false
  positive, but deliberately did *not* correct it — noted that unilaterally
  overriding a mechanically-reproducible rank is itself the kind of
  judgment-call divergence the incumbency rule exists to prevent, and
  recommended fixing the regex instead of relying on a human/agent to catch
  it every time.
- 2026-09-23 ~15:08 UTC: a later triage session (this one) did override it —
  demoted #8649 and promoted a genuine rank-3 candidate — then found it could
  not even self-revert because `urgent-flip-guard.sh`'s cooldown blocked the
  reversal. Net effect: two different sessions reached two different
  judgment calls on the identical false-positive input, which is the
  divergence-between-hosts failure mode the deterministic ladder exists to
  prevent in the first place.

## Fix

Require more context than a bare substring for the rank-2 pipeline-outage
match, e.g.:
- `\boutage\b` combined with an adjacent pipeline/CI noun (`pipeline
  outage`, `CI outage`, `build outage`), not a bare `outage` anywhere in the
  title, or
- Exclude common component-name collocations (`outage sentinel`, `outage
  detector`, `outage watcher`) explicitly, or
- Require the match to also NOT be immediately preceded by a noun suggesting
  it's a component/monitor name.

Update `.loom/roles/guide.md`'s (and `defaults/roles/guide.md`'s, per the
resync-source-of-truth convention noted elsewhere in that file)
`urgency_rank()` regex and its comment accordingly. Add a regression
fixture (mirroring the existing `test-guide-*` shell fixtures) asserting
that a title like "watchdog: peer-coord/outage sentinel writes silently
swallow I/O errors" ranks as tier-derived (3/4/5), not rank 2.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `urgency_rank()`'s rank-2 branch no longer matches on a bare `outage`
      (or `stalled`/`halted`/`wedged`) substring alone — it requires
      adjacent pipeline/CI/build context.
- [ ] A regression test fixture covers the #8649 title (or an equivalent
      "outage" component-name false positive) and asserts it does NOT rank 2.
- [ ] Existing genuine rank-2 titles ("main is red", "CI is red", "pipeline
      is stalled") still correctly rank 2 — no false negatives introduced.

issues.title: Auto-update: codesign timeout misclassified as tamper evidence in verify_darwin
issues.body:
## Bug Description

`loom-daemon`'s macOS auto-update signature check (`loom-daemon/src/release_fetch/signature.rs`, `verify_darwin`) treats a `codesign --verify --strict` invocation that **times out** identically to one that ran to completion and reported a genuinely invalid signature. Both fall through `CmdOutcome::succeeded()` returning `false` into the same `else` branch, which emits:

> macOS codesign verification FAILED for `<name>` -- an embedded signature is present but invalid. This is NOT the 'unsigned' case; treating as tamper evidence.

...and aborts the update. This conflates "we could not verify" with "we verified and it's bad" -- precisely the distinction `loom-daemon/src/cmd_out.rs` (this file's own dependency) exists to prevent. Its own module docs say of `Unavailable`: "The one outcome that means *we do not know*. Merging it into 'it failed' is how a wedged forge becomes an apparently-negative answer" -- but `verify_darwin`'s `else` branch does exactly that for its own `codesign --verify` call. `Unavailable::TimedOut`/`Unavailable::Collect` and a real `Ran` non-zero exit both fail `.succeeded()` and are indistinguishable in the `else` branch.

The first `codesign -dv` call (for the human-readable description) has the same gap: it checks for `Unavailable::Spawn` explicitly ("codesign not available") but not `Unavailable::TimedOut`, so a hang there just becomes an opaque `"timed out after ..."` string via `Unavailable::to_string()`, falls through the "code object is not signed at all" unsigned-skip check, and proceeds to the second call, which then also times out under the same contention and produces the tamper-evidence verdict.

## Reproduction Steps

1. On a host under heavy `syspolicyd`/`codesign`/CodeSigningHelper.xpc contention (observed here: 14 concurrent Loom sweep/role-runner agents plus other heavy processes), run `loom-daemon health` (or let the daemon's own auto-update tick fire). The `auto_update` line reports "macOS codesign verification FAILED ... tamper evidence" and aborts.
2. Independently verify this is a host-contention artifact, not a bad release artifact:
   - Downloaded `loom-daemon-aarch64-apple-darwin` fresh from the `v0.19.314` GitHub release and checked its `.sha256` -- checksum matched exactly (rules out corruption/tampering in transit).
   - Ran `codesign -dvv` / `codesign --verify --deep --strict --verbose=4` on the downloaded binary directly: both hung past 30s (`timeout 30 codesign -dvv ...` -> exit 124).
   - Control test: `timeout 20 codesign -dvv /usr/bin/codesign` (a stock, unquestionably-valid Apple system binary) **also hung and timed out**, proving the hang is host-side `codesign`/XPC contention, not anything about the downloaded artifact.
3. Read `loom-daemon/src/release_fetch/signature.rs::verify_darwin` and `loom-daemon/src/release_fetch/signature/tests.rs`: the only "signed but invalid" test (`macos_signed_but_invalid_fails_closed`) uses a fake `codesign` script that exits 1 deterministically with a real invalid-signature message -- there is no test coverage for the `Unavailable::TimedOut`/`Unavailable::Collect` path from either `codesign` invocation in this function.

## Expected Behavior

A `codesign` invocation that times out or otherwise can't be collected should report an inconclusive/unavailable outcome (soft-skip or retry, analogous to the existing `Unavailable::Spawn` -> "codesign not available" handling a few lines above), not the same hard-fail "tamper evidence" verdict reserved for a `codesign` run that actually completed and reported an invalid signature.

## Actual Behavior

A timeout is reported as "an embedded signature is present but invalid ... treating as tamper evidence," which is misleading (no signature was actually found to be invalid -- verification simply never completed) and blocks the fleet's auto-update indefinitely under load without ever distinguishing the two cases.

## Environment

- OS: Darwin 27.0.0 (arm64)
- Commit: 0c66c5696315ea61d9ea77d634f94849c2ad6ba2 (origin/main, VERSION 0.19.315)
- Installed daemon binary on this host: 0.19.307 -- stuck there because this bug keeps rejecting every subsequent release artifact's auto-update attempt under host load

## Impact

Blocks this host's `loom-daemon` auto-update indefinitely whenever the host is busy enough to make `codesign` slow (a common state on this fleet host, which runs many concurrent sweep/role-runner agents) -- and does so with alarming, incorrect "tamper evidence" language that could cause an operator to distrust a legitimate release. CI passed on `main` at HEAD; this is a runtime/self-update-path bug, not a build or test failure.

---
Discovered during main branch audit.

issues.title: feat(dashboard): visual timeline dashboard for Loom lifecycle and token usage over time
issues.body:
<details>
<summary>Original issue (preserved)</summary>

### Problem Statement
Operators currently lack an at-a-glance web view on the Loom dashboard (`https://dashboard.2amlogic.com`) to visualize token throughput (tokens/min), % capacity saturation, and end-to-end issue lifecycle progression.

### Proposed Solution
Add interactive time-series plots and lifecycle waterfall views to the web dashboard backed by local OTLP/SigNoz metrics.

---
**Operator Priority Bump** (comment by @2ambots, 2026-09-26): Promoted to `tier:goal-advancing` and `priority:high` by @turian via Chat-Ops.

</details>

---

<!-- loom:complexity=routine -->

## Curator Enhancement

### Problem Statement (clarified)

The operator's framing names a concrete target: **`dashboard.2amlogic.com`**. That
hostname is **not** the embedded `loom-daemon serve` HTML dashboard (the
loopback-only, port-7420, no-build-toolchain page compiled into the daemon
binary — see `.loom/docs/daemon-reference.md` §"Fleet dashboard"). It is the
**reference deployment of the `dashboard/` Cloudflare Workers app**
(`loom-observability-backend` — ingest + D1 history + a `FleetState` Durable
Object + the Phase-3 UI in `dashboard/web/`), confirmed by `CHANGELOG.md`
("Reference deployment: dashboard.2amlogic.com") and `WORK_LOG.md` ("2AM
production deploy: dashboard.2amlogic.com cutover", issue #4859). All work
below targets `dashboard/web/src/`, not `loom-daemon/src/serve.rs`.

**Correction to the original "Proposed Solution":** it says the dashboard is
"backed by local OTLP/SigNoz metrics." That's a different, parallel effort —
SigNoz/ClickStack/HyperDX is a *separate* telemetry trial (epics #8522/#8529,
`.loom/docs/observability.md`, `ci-observability.md`) with no wiring to
`dashboard.2amlogic.com`. The dashboard's actual data path is
`loom-daemon`'s own native `HttpsExporter`
(`loom-daemon/src/observability/exporter.rs`) pushing to the Workers
`/ingest` route, not OTLP/SigNoz. This issue's work has no dependency on the
SigNoz effort.

**This dashboard already has substantially more built than the issue as filed
implies.** Before scoping work, here is what already exists (epic #4702,
issues #4726/#4750/#4751/#4752/#4753/#4847/#4998/#8852):

- **Per-sweep lifecycle timelines** (`web/src/sweepTimelineView.ts` +
  `timelineBuilder.ts`, issue #4750): phase progression
  curator → builder → judge → doctor → merge, per sweep, with durations and
  PR link.
- **Historical charts** (`web/src/historicalChartsPanel.ts`, issue #4751):
  outcomes-over-time, success-rate trend, duration percentiles — full
  interactive charts (dated axis, hover tooltip, accessible table fallback)
  via `web/src/charts/chartChrome.ts`.
- **Per-host sweep-throughput and health-trend charts**
  (`web/src/hostHistoryPanel.ts`).
- **Token/cost analytics** (`web/src/analytics/*`, issue #4752): per-account
  burn curves (`burn.ts`), exhaustion forecasts including a computed
  **burn-rate `slopePerHour`** (`forecast.ts`), per-repo attribution
  (`attribution.ts`), and — **already rendering today, on both the
  authenticated and public surface** — a **"Fleet token-pool load" panel**
  (`web/src/analytics/render.ts`'s `renderPoolBurn`/`renderPoolBurnCard`)
  that draws a small SVG **sparkline of peak/mean `usage_fraction` (i.e. %
  pool capacity) over time, per host, 0–100%-pinned**
  (`renderPoolSparkline`).
- A CPU/load **saturation badge** per host (`idle`/`elevated`/`critical`,
  issue #4998, `src/publicPage.ts`) — a *different* kind of "saturation"
  (CPU load, not token/dispatch capacity).

So the literal phrase "% saturation UI panel" for token usage is **partially
already shipped** as a decorative sparkline. What is genuinely missing, and
what this issue should scope to, is narrower than the original title
suggests.

### What's actually missing (the real gap)

1. **No rolling *rate* (throughput) visualization exists anywhere.**
   `forecast.ts` computes `slopePerHour` (usage_fraction consumed per hour,
   least-squares fit over the live burn segment) purely to project an
   exhaustion ETA — it is never plotted as its own time series. There is a
   ready-made formatter for it (`analytics/format.ts`'s `formatRatePerHour`
   → `"N.N%/h"`) but no chart.
2. **The existing pool-load sparkline is decorative, not a first-class
   chart.** It is a bare inline SVG (`renderPoolSparkline`) with no dated
   x-axis, no hover tooltip, and no `renderTableView` accessible fallback —
   unlike the three real charts in `historicalChartsPanel.ts`, which all use
   `charts/chartChrome.ts` for exactly that chrome.
3. **"Tokens/min" is not a representable unit.** Per
   `dashboard/docs/token-analytics.md` (§"Units are limit-window
   fractions"): *"No absolute token count or price exists anywhere in the
   telemetry, so none is synthesized."* `tokens.snapshot` (see
   `.loom/docs/telemetry-schema.md`) carries only `usage_fraction` (a
   fraction of a rolling rate-limit window) per account, never a raw token
   count. Any "rolling token throughput" panel must be honestly labeled as a
   **burn *rate*** (`%` of pool capacity per hour), not tokens/minute — the
   operator's Chat-Ops phrasing ("tokens/min") does not match what the data
   model can support, and the panel must not imply a unit it cannot back.
4. **No dispatch/concurrency-capacity saturation view.** `queue.snapshot`
   (schema v11, `.loom/docs/telemetry-schema.md`) already carries
   `max_concurrent` (the concurrency cap a tick ran under) and
   `counts.running`, and — like every ingested record — is persisted
   unconditionally to D1 by `handleIngest` in `dashboard/src/index.ts`
   (regardless of `kind`), so `running / max_concurrent` over time is
   *already queryable* via `/api/history`/`/public/history` with **zero
   backend changes**. This is a second, orthogonal "% capacity saturation"
   signal (compute/dispatch capacity, not token-pool capacity) and is
   explicitly **out of scope** for this issue (see Overlap note below).
5. **No fleet-wide multi-sweep "lifecycle waterfall".** The existing
   `sweepTimelineView.ts` renders one sweep's phase list at a time. A
   Gantt/waterfall view of *concurrent* sweeps across the fleet (the
   original issue's "Proposed Solution" language) is a materially larger UI
   feature than a single chart.

### Overlap with sibling issue #9032 (being curated in parallel)

#9032 ("expose dedicated org-wide ranked ready dispatch queue view
`/dashboard/queue`") targets the **same repo directory** and, notably, a
route (`/#/queue`) that **already exists**: `web/src/views/workQueue.ts`'s
`workQueueView` already renders a live running/ready/blocked queue at that
hash route (issue #8852, phase 3), backed by `queue.snapshot` — though
#9032's proposed backend (`GET /api/v1/queue/ranked`, a fresh org-wide
GitHub-issue ranking by `work_finder::candidate_cmp`) is not obviously the
same data source. Whoever curates/builds #9032 needs to reconcile that
overlap; it is out of scope for #9029 to resolve. **For this issue:** do not
touch `web/src/views/workQueue.ts`, `web/src/workQueue.ts`,
`web/src/queueTypes.ts`, or the `#/queue` route — the chart this issue adds
lives in `web/src/analytics/` and/or `web/src/charts/`, a disjoint file set.

### Acceptance Criteria (single-PR core)

Build **one** new chart: a **rolling token-pool burn-rate ("throughput")
chart** — the genuinely net-new piece named in the operator's framing.

- [ ] A new derivation function (e.g. `web/src/analytics/burnRate.ts` or
      added to `burn.ts`) computes a **bounded rolling-window rate** (%
      pool-capacity-per-hour) from `PoolBurnCurve`/`PoolBurnPoint` data
      (`web/src/analytics/burn.ts`), reusing the existing segment
      boundaries (`buildPoolBurnCurves`' rollover/gap segmentation) so a
      limit-window reset never reads as a throughput cliff or a fabricated
      negative rate.
- [ ] The rolling window is a named, bounded constant/option (no unbounded
      in-memory accumulation) — consistent with the existing
      `DEFAULT_WINDOW_DAYS` / `CHART_PAGE_SIZE` bounding pattern in
      `web/src/historicalChartsPanel.ts`.
- [ ] A new chart-view module renders the rate series as a **first-class
      interactive chart** using `web/src/charts/chartChrome.ts` (dated
      x-axis, y-axis, hover tooltip, `renderTableView` accessible
      fallback) — matching `web/src/charts/successRateChartView.ts`'s
      pattern, not a bare decorative sparkline like the existing
      `renderPoolSparkline`.
- [ ] The panel/axis/labels call the metric a **burn rate** (`%/h`, reusing
      `analytics/format.ts`'s existing `formatRatePerHour`) — never
      "tokens/min" or any absolute token count.
- [ ] Renders on **both** the authenticated (`/api/history`) and public
      (`/public/history`) surfaces, matching the existing pool-level
      public-exposure precedent in `docs/token-analytics.md` (§2): pool
      aggregate fields (`mean_usage_fraction`/`max_usage_fraction`/
      `exhausted_count`) are already public-safe. The new chart must **not**
      introduce any per-account or per-repo identity onto the public
      surface — no changes to `src/redaction.ts` should be needed; if the
      implementation finds it needs one, that is a sign the metric chosen
      is per-account, not pool-level, and the design should be revisited.
- [ ] No changes to `dashboard/src/index.ts` (ingest), `src/query.ts`, D1
      migrations, or `src/redaction.ts` — every input this chart needs is
      already ingested and queryable today.
- [ ] New unit tests for both the rate-derivation function and the
      chart-view render, following the existing pairing convention
      (`web/test/successRate.test.ts` + `successRateChartView.test.ts`),
      including a test asserting a limit-window rollover does not produce a
      spurious large-negative rate point.
- [ ] `npm --prefix dashboard test` and `npm --prefix dashboard/web test`
      (or the repo's `npm run check:all` in `dashboard/`) pass. **Do not run
      `cargo` anywhere for this issue — it is a TypeScript/Workers-only
      change.**

### Explicitly out of scope (documented follow-ups, not filed as issues)

1. **Upgrade the existing decorative pool-load sparkline**
   (`renderPoolBurn`/`renderPoolSparkline` in
   `web/src/analytics/render.ts`) to the same `chartChrome.ts` chrome as
   the new rate chart — arguably the more literal reading of "% saturation
   UI panel", but deliberately deferred so this PR stays to one new chart.
2. **Dispatch/concurrency capacity saturation** (`queue.snapshot`'s
   `counts.running / max_concurrent`, per-host and fleet-wide, over time) —
   a second, legitimate "% capacity saturation" signal, already fully
   queryable historically with zero backend changes. Deferred to avoid
   `web/src/views/workQueue.ts` file overlap with #9032 until that issue's
   scope settles.
3. **Fleet-wide multi-sweep "lifecycle waterfall" / Gantt view** — the
   original issue's "lifecycle waterfall" phrase. Materially larger than a
   single chart; `sweepTimelineView.ts` only covers one sweep at a time
   today.
4. **Live SSE-driven auto-refresh** of the new chart (the existing
   `HistoricalChartsPanel` pattern re-fetches `/api/history` on filter
   change, not via the live event tail in `sseFeedClient.ts`) — nice-to-have,
   not required for acceptance.

### Affected files (expected)

- `dashboard/web/src/analytics/burn.ts` or a new `analytics/burnRate.ts` —
  rate derivation
- `dashboard/web/src/analytics/render.ts` — mount the new chart alongside
  the existing pool blocks
- A new `dashboard/web/src/charts/*ChartView.ts` (or an `analytics/`-local
  equivalent) reusing `charts/chartChrome.ts`
- `dashboard/web/test/*` — new test files per the pairing convention above
- `dashboard/docs/token-analytics.md` — document the new rate metric next
  to the existing burn-curve/forecast documentation (small doc update, same
  file the existing burn-curve public-exposure decision already lives in)

### Test Plan

- [ ] Automated: unit tests for rate derivation (including the
      segment-boundary/rollover case) and for the chart-view render
      (following `successRateChartView.test.ts`'s structure).
- [ ] Manual: `npm --prefix dashboard run dev`, seed a host with a few
      `tokens.snapshot` samples spanning a rollover (see the `README.md`
      "Local development" `curl` recipe), confirm the new chart renders on
      both `/` (authenticated) and the public variant without per-account
      data leaking into the public response.
- [ ] Edge cases: fewer than 2 samples in range (no chart / explicit
      no-data state, not a crash); a rollover mid-window; a multi-host pool.
